# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

# Weekly Review

Step back, look at the week, and plan the next one.

## When to Use

Run this once a week — Sunday evening, Monday morning, or whenever works for your rhythm.

## Instructions

### Step 1 - Gather
1. Check this week's calendar events (if calendar MCP is connected).
2. Review completed tasks or projects from the week.
3. Scan any notes, journal entries, or captured items from the past seven days.
4. **Email digest via the Gmail MCP** (see `Skills/Comms/gmail-triage/SKILL.md` for conventions). Report counts per category - don't list individual emails unless Mark asks. Use `search_threads`:
   - Important unread (7d): `is:unread is:important in:inbox newer_than:7d`
   - Primary/people unread (7d): `is:unread in:inbox category:primary newer_than:7d`
   - Notifications unread (7d): `is:unread in:inbox category:updates newer_than:7d`
   - Newsletters (7d): `in:inbox category:promotions newer_than:7d`

   (Meeting-transcript listing retired with Spark; there is no Gmail equivalent.)
5. **Writing Kanban review.** Open the APR Kanban view mentally - ask Mark which items he wants to commit to this week. Convert commitments into OmniFocus tasks via `omnifocus-capture`. The Kanban stays as idea pool + writing-capture; the weekly picks go to OmniFocus.
6. **Marketing Experiments check.** Skim `APR/Analytics/Experiments/_Experiments Index.md` for active experiments. Flag any whose monitoring dates have arrived.
7. **Repo work recap (what shipped).** Read-only git history across Mark's APR repos to summarize the week's shipped work. Repos:
   - APR astro (website): `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro` (usually the bulk of the work; descriptive commit messages)
   - social-media-posting: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/social-media-posting` (evergreen/batch posting tooling; low volume)

   **Excluded - LifeHQ-Mark** (`/Users/marklevison/Documents/Obsidian/LifeHQ-Mark`): a global deny rule blocks Read/Edit/Write on it (set in `~/.claude/settings.json`), and it is all "Autocommit" vault backups anyway. Do not try to read it. If Mark asks why it is missing, point at the deny rule.

   For each repo, run (use `git -C <path>`, not `cd` - `cd` resets the shell cwd and can trip a permission prompt):
   ```bash
   # Commit list with messages
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --date=short --pretty=format:"%ad | %s"
   # Per-commit scope, for sizing the work
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --pretty=format:"%h %s" --shortstat
   # Area churn (which folders moved the most)
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --pretty=format: --name-only \
     | grep -v '^$' | sed 's:/[^/]*$::' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30
   ```
   Default window is the last 7 days (today minus 7); honor an explicit range if Mark gives one. Then:
   - Group commits into 2-5 themes per repo (e.g. email/CRM, funnel/quiz, sales pages, analytics refresh, course logistics). Lead with outcomes, not commit subjects.

8. **OmniFocus inbox sweep.** Run `omnifocus-inbox-triage` to clear the OmniFocus inbox — walk each item, propose a project (plus tags/due/flag as needed), and apply approved edits as a batch. See `Skills/OmniFocus/inbox-triage/SKILL.md`. Skip if the inbox is empty; note the count either way.
9. **Drafts review and cleanup.** Run `drafts-inbox` to process the Drafts inbox — read each captured item, take the action, and archive when done. See `Skills/Comms/drafts-inbox/SKILL.md`. Skip if the inbox is empty; note the count either way.
10. **Content Ideas resurfacing.** Read `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` and surface 2-3 hooks for Mark to consider promoting into Writing Tasks (`APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/`) or this week's plan. Rotate which ones you highlight so the whole list stays in view over time. Skip if the note is empty or missing.

### Step 2 — Review
1. Summarize what happened this week: key events, completed work, progress made.
2. Identify what's still open: tasks that didn't get finished, items that slipped.
3. Flag anything overdue or time-sensitive.

### Step 3 — Output
Produce a formatted weekly summary **in chat only**. This is an in-the-moment review — do not save it to a file, and do not ask reflective questions.

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

6	# Content Ideas
7	
8	Running list of quick hooks and angles for blog, newsletter, and social. Captured from the Drafts inbox triage. Review periodically and promote the good ones into Writing Tasks (`APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/`).
9	
10	## Hooks
11	
12	- **If we implemented every feature in your product backlog today, would your users be happy?** A provocative backlog-as-value question. (captured 2026-06-11)
13	- **BDD was always about the collaboration.** If you just use Given / When / Then to feed an LLM, it's a prompt with pretty formatting. (BDD + GenAI angle, captured 2026-06-04)
14	- **GenAI handles computer tasks fine; the more a question touches the real world or human emotions, the less reliable it gets.** (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-07-05)
15	- **Maximizing token budget is silly, going faster doesn't make you more productive.** (AI productivity angle, captured 2026-07-05)
16	- **Reasoning models don't reason.** Current-generation "reasoning" is statistical pattern matching, replaying patterns from training data, not logical deduction. More effective than non-reasoning models, but still a stochastic parrot. (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-02-11)
17	
18	## Scrum / PM scenario bank
19	
20	Real-world organizational-challenge scenarios, each rich enough for a full post or Scrum-by-Example episode. (captured 2026-01-16 from Drafts triage)
21	
22	- **Old guard vs new guard.** Veterans refuse to merge until a whole Epic is reviewed; newcomers want frequent merges. Result: merge hell and integration errors.
23	- **The sunk-cost negotiation trap.** Customer deliberately slows the sales process until the project is ~75% done, then threatens cancellation to force a discount.
24	- **The "dead horse" retrospective ban.** Management bans recurring external impediments (e.g. a slow third-party supplier) from retrospective discussion.
25	- **Specialization within a team.** 12 devs, each a one-person show on a separate submodule, so code reviews lack the expertise to be meaningful.
26	- **The "status pull" efficiency argument.** How to show a manager that whole-team status-report meetings are waste, even when the manager finds them convenient.
27	- **The "Tom" problem.** A senior dev delivers 80% of a task, overrides the wireframe (green button, not blue), and adds unplanned features like login animations.
28	- **Revenue-impacting bug priority.** A colleague wants a new "impacts revenue" bug category, making everything crisis-urgent and crowding out other work.
29	- **Larry vs Winston working hours.** "Laid-back Larry" is stressed by an 8-hour day and needs breaks; "workaholic Winston" feels he's carrying a free-rider.
30	- **The single-point-of-contact tool conflict.** A contractual single-point-of-contact clause collides with tools (e.g. Basecamp) that invite many-to-many communication.
31	- **The vicious firefighting cycle.** POs and support constantly pull devs off the Sprint Goal to fix setups or recover data.
32	- **The zero-sum KPI game.** Engineer's KPI (pass QA bug-free) and tester's KPI (find more bugs) create a conflict of interest that hurts morale.
33	- **The specialist utilization problem.** An "adopted expert" (e.g. a UX guru) has only ~10% of a Sprint's work but is required at every standup with no outside interruptions.
34	- **Project vs process in maintenance.** How to define a PM's role when management assigns a PM to a maintenance team whose work has no distinct end.
35	- **Delayed information from customers.** 60 stories are dev-done but can't be closed because an unresponsive customer has been sitting on needed info for weeks.

# Content Ideas

Running list of quick hooks and angles for blog, newsletter, and social. Captured from the Drafts inbox triage. Review periodically and promote the good ones into Writing Tasks (`APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/`).

## Hooks

- **If we implemented every feature in your product backlog today, would your users be happy?** A provocative backlog-as-value question. (captured 2026-06-11)
- **BDD was always about the collaboration.** If you just use Given / When / Then to feed an LLM, it's a prompt with pretty formatting. (BDD + GenAI angle, captured 2026-06-04)
- **GenAI handles computer tasks fine; the more a question touches the real world or human emotions, the less reliable it gets.** (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-07-05)
- **Maximizing token budget is silly, going faster doesn't make you more productive.** (AI productivity angle, captured 2026-07-05)
- **Reasoning models don't reason.** Current-generation "reasoning" is statistical pattern matching, replaying patterns from training data, not logical deduction. More effective than non-reasoning models, but still a stochastic parrot. (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-02-11)

## Scrum / PM scenario bank

Real-world organizational-challenge scenarios, each rich enough for a full post or Scrum-by-Example episode. (captured 2026-01-16 from Drafts triage)

- **Old guard vs new guard.** Veterans refuse to merge until a whole Epic is reviewed; newcomers want frequent merges. Result: merge hell and integration errors.
- **The sunk-cost negotiation trap.** Customer deliberately slows the sales process until the project is ~75% done, then threatens cancellation to force a discount.
- **The "dead horse" retrospective ban.** Management bans recurring external impediments (e.g. a slow third-party supplier) from retrospective discussion.
- **Specialization within a team.** 12 devs, each a one-person show on a separate submodule, so code reviews lack the expertise to be meaningful.
- **The "status pull" efficiency argument.** How to show a manager that whole-team status-report meetings are waste, even when the manager finds them convenient.
- **The "Tom" problem.** A senior dev delivers 80% of a task, overrides the wireframe (green button, not blue), and adds unplanned features like login animations.
- **Revenue-impacting bug priority.** A colleague wants a new "impacts revenue" bug category, making everything crisis-urgent and crowding out other work.
- **Larry vs Winston working hours.** "Laid-back Larry" is stressed by an 8-hour day and needs breaks; "workaholic Winston" feels he's carrying a free-rider.
- **The single-point-of-contact tool conflict.** A contractual single-point-of-contact clause collides with tools (e.g. Basecamp) that invite many-to-many communication.
- **The vicious firefighting cycle.** POs and support constantly pull devs off the Sprint Goal to fix setups or recover data.
- **The zero-sum KPI game.** Engineer's KPI (pass QA bug-free) and tester's KPI (find more bugs) create a conflict of interest that hurts morale.
- **The specialist utilization problem.** An "adopted expert" (e.g. a UX guru) has only ~10% of a Sprint's work but is required at every standup with no outside interruptions.
- **Project vs process in maintenance.** How to define a PM's role when management assigns a PM to a maintenance team whose work has no distinct end.
- **Delayed information from customers.** 60 stories are dev-done but can't be closed because an unresponsive customer has been sitting on needed info for weeks.
